Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.
  • The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security.
  • According to recent reports, what do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

The International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds that the push to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels is accelerating electrification and the shift toward domestic energy sources, including renewables. Yet electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and concerns about energy security are also giving coal a longer life in some countries. The IEA warns that the pursuit of energy security alone won’t deliver the emissions reductions needed to meet global climate goals.

According to recent reports, what do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts? Nick Wayth, global director of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, explains four key takeaways from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

According to recent reports, Q: How close will current and proposed policies get us to the COP31 pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035? What changes are needed to bridge the gap?

The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for electrification as a way for countries to diversify their power sources and reduce dependence on imports, improving energy security and affordability. While the world’s reliance on fossil fuels hasn’t changed substantially, there’s been a real shift in how countries think about the risks of that dependence—and the benefits of electrification. But progress is too slow. The IEA projects that under current and proposed policies, electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035. That’s only half the increase needed to reach the COP31 target of 35%.

In a recent development, much of the technology is already available. The IEA estimates that nearly half of fossil fuel demand in road transport and more than a third of demand for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at a competitive cost today. The challenge is creating the conditions for businesses and households to make that switch.

Recent findings suggest that to reach the target, countries need to develop detailed plans for shifting transport, heating, and heavy industry toward electricity and invest in transmission and distribution. Governments can help keep their industries competitive by making it more attractive for businesses to switch from gas to affordable electricity. Some countries are doing this successfully already. Germany, for example, has reduced electricity taxes for manufacturers and has subsidized grid charges, helping lower electricity costs for businesses.

Q: The IEA projects rapid growth in electricity demand from both air conditioning and data centers. How do the challenges posed by these two sources of demand differ?

It has been revealed that energy demand from AI and data centers has dominated public attention this year, but by 2035 the global growth in electricity demand from cooling is forecast to be about 70% greater than from data centers. Notably, the IEA finds that global demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating them for the first time in history.

In a recent development, energy demand from data centers is concentrated in the U.S., China, and the EU. By contrast, demand for cooling is widespread, especially in emerging and developing economies where much of the population is vulnerable to extreme heat, an increasing threat to human life.

Recent findings suggest that under current and proposed government policies, cooling is projected to account for 12% of global electricity consumption by 2035. But during periods of peak demand, when millions of air conditioners are running at once, it could reach around 30% of the electricity needed. Electricity grids must be able to cope with these spikes in demand, even if they occur only occasionally. Without better planning and more efficient cooling, countries could face costly grid upgrades—or risk power outages during extreme heat.

This is why policymakers and utilities need to anticipate future electricity demand and proposal investments in grid infrastructure accordingly. But building more isn’t the only solution. Governments and utilities should also invest in energy storage and other grid flexibility measures that enable them to adapt to fluctuating supply and demand as needed.

It has been revealed that Q: The energy crisis is accelerating clean electrification in some countries but also encouraging greater reliance on fossil fuels in others. What does the IEA’s outlook tell us about the future of oil, coal, and gas—and the risks of investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure?

According to recent reports, the report indicates that global oil demand is expected to level off by 2030 under current and proposed policies. The slowdown in China’s oil demand, driven largely by electric vehicle adoption, is expected to continue. Other fast-growing economies, such as India, despite electrifying transport, are nonetheless projected to increase their demand for oil.

Recent findings suggest that the current energy crisis is reinforcing these differences in strategy. Some countries are investing in electrification to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, while others are turning to domestic fossil fuels.

The energy crisis has given coal demand a short-term boost, and the IEA now expects coal use in 2035 to be higher than it projected just a year ago. Even so, under current and proposed government policies, global coal demand is expected to fall by 14% between 2025 and 2035, driven largely by a decline in coal-fired power generation, particularly in China. But coal use in industry is projected to fall by just 5%, highlighting the challenge of reducing dependence on the fuel.

Countries need to be cautious about investing in infrastructure that may not be needed. The IEA estimates that about 400 billion cubic meters (bcm) of fresh liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity is under construction and could come online by 2035. Yet under current and stated government policies, export capacity could significantly exceed demand in 2035 by70 bcm. That surplus raises the risk of underused infrastructure and investments that fail to pay off.

It has been revealed that the IEA estimates that the world will need at least 25 million kilometers of newly introduced power lines over the next decade to meet growing electricity demand and connect new sources of power, including renewables. Another 15 million kilometers of existing lines will need to be upgraded or replaced. Both will require substantial investment.

Sources indicate that the biggest challenge is delivering these changes fast enough. Major grid projects can take 5 to15 years to plan, secure permits for, and complete—far longer than many renewable energy projects. Governments need to speed up permitting and grid connections, improve coordination between utilities and developers, and encourage investment before demand materializes. One encouraging example is the EU’s recent provisional agreement to streamline permitting for grid projects.

Equally important is to invest in ways to use existing assets more efficiently. Grid-enhancing technologies can speed up connections by allowing existing power lines to carry more electricity, reducing the need to build fresh infrastructure. And increasingly, governments and utilities are seeing the importance of making grids more flexible—building in capability and strategies to balance supply with demand in real time. Brazil, for example, pays large electricity consumers to temporarily reduce consumption when the grid is under strain. Businesses that fail to deliver the agreed reductions can lose payments or face suspension from programs. By combining energy storage, demand-response programs, smart grid controls, distributed energy generation, and other flexibility strategies, energy planners can meet growing demands and increase resilience while reducing the need to build more grid infrastructure.

Industry observers note that courtesy of WRI. By Sarah George, Senior Manager, Strategic Communications, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; and Francisco Boshell, Global Lead, Decarbonized Energy Consumption, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DTE Energy recently declared plans to add up to 150 megawatts of newly introduced solar energy in Michigan, a move that will create construction jobs, support local communities, and save customers money on fuel costs, the manufacturer noted.

In addition, because solar generation does not require fuel, the latest projects will help reduce the tech giant’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

Sources indicate that the tech giant stated that these projects are an investment in Michigan and its communities. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require the purchase  of fuel, it can help lower energy costs for customers and reduce the reliance on fuel from outside the state. At the same time, these projects will create jobs and bring new investment and tax revenue into local communities, providing more resources for schools, first responders and the services Michigan families count on every day.

DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of new Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

Projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

DTE is a producer of and investor in renewable energy in Michigan, generating enough clean energy from wind and solar to power nearly one million homes. As the company works toward net zero carbon emissions, it remains committed to growing its renewable energy portfolio while maintaining a balanced mix of energy resources that supports reliability and affordability for customers. DTE’s 2026 Integrated Resource Proposal builds on that commitment, calling for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042.

Breaking: The Legendary 1987 RUF CTR 'Yellowbird' Looks Like A Porsche, But It Isn't

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, take a quick look at that yellow beast in our top photo, with its bulging muscular fenders, curved profile, and massive whale tail spoiler.
  • Industry observers note that there are a couple of dead giveaways, too, including the fact that the Yellowbird could outrun any real production Porsches of the time.
  • In a recent development, of course, peeking under the skin of the Yellowbird tells the tale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, take a quick look at that yellow beast in our top photo, with its bulging muscular fenders, curved profile, and massive whale tail spoiler. Now, you could easily be forgiven for thinking it was a Porsche — perhaps a late-1980s 911 Carrera 3.2. You'd be wrong, however. That machine is actually a Ruf CTR, which was nicknamed the Yellowbird for its striking exterior finish.

Industry observers note that there are a couple of dead giveaways, too, including the fact that the Yellowbird could outrun any real production Porsches of the time. In fact, a Ruf CTR beat all challengers at a famed 1987 Road & Track comparison of the fastest cars in the world: Its 211-mph top speed was 10 mph faster than the second-place car, which was a modified Porsche, while entries like the AMG Hammer, Ferrari Testarossa, Lamborghini Countach, and Porsche 959 all failed to reach 200 mph. Unsurprisingly, the CTR was also named one of our readers' favorite yellow cars of all time.

In a recent development, of course, peeking under the skin of the Yellowbird tells the tale. Keep in mind that Ruf is much more than just a tuning shop or an in-house performance brand, like Mercedes' AMG was and now is. Ruf uses so many proprietary components — and so few from production Porsche models — that it was certified as a full-on automaker back in 1981. Ruf cars even have different W09 VINs from Porsche's WP0 vehicle identification numbers. The genesis, though, actually does start with a Mercedes-Benz — well, that and a Porsche 356.

The company now known as Ruf — pronounced roof – began when Alois Ruf Sr. opened his first repair shop in Pfaffenhausen, Germany, in 1939. Ruf and the shop would both survive World War II, and in the 1950s, he expanded into building his own tour bus — on a chassis originally sourced from Mercedes-Benz.

It was in 1963, when Ruf was at the wheel of his bus, that he happened to see a driver lose control of his Porsche 356 and run off the road. Ruf then played a key role in bringing both back to health: He drove the Porsche's owner to the hospital and — after buying it off of the insurer — took the car itself back to his shop to fix. That began a lifelong romance between the Rufs and rear-engined Porsches, and one that carried over to the launch of the 911. Today, 911s like the Carrera GTS T-Hybrid are still out there making the haters look real dumb.

According to recent reports, we're going to skip a lot of steps in a pretty fascinating story, but Alois Jr. took over for his father in 1974 after the latter died. Under Alois Jr.'s direction, and in response to rumors Porsche would kill off the 911 after introducing the front-engine 928, the company committed itself to supporting the 911 even if Porsche didn't. The first Ruf-tuned 911, the Turbo 3.3, premiered in 1977 with a Ruf-built 5-speed manual transmission. However, legal worries soon reared their ugly heads. Porsche, naturally, wasn't too keen on being liable for what Ruf did to its cars, so Ruf would go on to officially become an independent automaker in 1981.

Yet, the car that really put Ruf on the map was the 1987 CTR, with a name derived from "Group C Turbo Ruf." The car started life as a 930-series 911 Carrera with a 3.2-liter flat-six engine, which was already one of the lightest models on the Porsche roster — it just wasn't light enough for Ruf. The company swapped out the production doors, engine cover, and bumpers to save more poundage. The car even has just one sideview mirror. The rear fenders also were reworked, with flares to handle its upsized tire/wheel package and NACA ducts for engine cooling.

Ruf increased the bore of the Carrera's donor engine as well, boosting displacement to 3.4 liters. Remember, bore and stroke are the two specs that decide an engine's power. Next up were twin-turbochargers custom made for the Yellowbird and Bosch fuel injectors to slake the motor's thirst. The result was 469 horsepower and 408 pound-feet of torque. The 1987 Porsche 959, for some perspective, came out with a twin-turbo 2.8-liter flat-six factory rated for 444 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque.

The differences were even more noticeable on the track, as mentioned above. We'll also add that while the 959 was a tenth quicker to 60, at 3.6 seconds, the CTR could keep on going to reach 100 mph in 7.3 seconds. That's 1.5 seconds quicker than the 959. But if you really want to get a feel for what the Yellowbird was all about, be sure to check out Weissach Group's video of Ruf driver Stefan Roser running one at Nürburgring in 1989. It's downright fascinating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exhaust tips are the most visible parts of a car's exhaust system, making them a worthwhile option if you want to personalize your ride without spending a big chunk of cash on a complete aftermarket exhaust setup — especially if you don't want to risk voiding your warranty and ruining the mental peace of your neighbors. Available in different shapes, sizes, materials, and finishes, aftermarket exhaust tips can lend a sportier or more premium appearance to the car they're fitted to.

That said, some believe that in addition to the aesthetic uplift, aftermarket tips can produce a deeper or louder exhaust note, help direct hot exhaust gases away from the rear bumper, and even improve your car's performance by reducing backpressure. What's fact, what's fiction, and do these benefits justify upgrading your car's factory exhaust tips?

The short answer is that aftermarket exhaust tips can offer some practical advantages, but they have next to no impact on performance and only a subtle effect on sound, at best. To understand what you gain from replacing them, it is important to distinguish between the exhaust tip and the components that actually determine how an exhaust system works.

It has been revealed that unlike the muffler, resonator, or catalytic converter, the exhaust tip doesn't really play a significant role in controlling exhaust noise, emissions, or gas flow through your car's exhaust system. Its primary purpose is to finish the exhaust outlet, which is why aftermarket tips are available in several designs. These include straight-cut, angle-cut, rolled-edge, dual-exit, turndown, resonated, and dual-wall tips. Owners can also choose between finishes like polished stainless steel, chrome, matte black, and carbonfiber-like materials. Most aftermarket exhaust tips are pretty straightforward to install, with clamp-on and slip-on designs that directly attach to the existing tailpipe.

There can be a minor change in exhaust sound, depending on the tip's diameter, length, shape, and the material used. A larger outlet may produce a somewhat deeper tone, while a longer tip can make your exhaust sound a little bit softer. A turndown tip directs exhaust gases and sound toward the ground, whereas a resonated tip can help reduce raspiness. To sum up, don't expect an aftermarket exhaust tip to make your daily-driver Toyota Camry sound like a V8-powered Lexus RC F.

Recent findings suggest that one possible practical upside to an aftermarket exhaust tip is that it can help direct hot exhaust gases away from the bumper and surrounding body panels, and reduce soot accumulation around the outlet (particularly if you drive a diesel car), provided it is correctly sized and positioned. Stainless steel tips can additionally offer better rust resistance than some factory exhaust tips.

Industry observers note that despite what the marketing for some aftermarket exhaust tips may suggest, using them does not deliver a noticeable increase in power, torque, or overall performance. A common misconception is that a larger-diameter tip reduces exhaust backpressure, reducing the strain on the engine and thereby producing more power. However, since the tip is only the final outlet of the exhaust system, it has no effect on the system's overall flow characteristics. The diameter, length, and layout of the exhaust pipes, along with the design of the catalytic converter, muffler, and resonator, have a much greater impact.

Sources indicate that if you're looking for more noticeable changes in sound or performance, your best bet is to upgrade other components of the exhaust system. A performance muffler can deliver a more aggressive exhaust note and reduce backpressure, while an aftermarket resonator can give you finer control over sound. A cat-back exhaust system replaces the components from the catalytic converter to the tailpipe and can also offer a substantial change in sound and performance by dialing up the exhaust flow. Upgraded headers and high-flow catalytic converters are a couple more viable options to get a more aggressive exhaust note and boost performance.

That said, these modifications are considerably more expensive than an aftermarket exhaust tip, and may affect emissions compliance and noise levels, possibly even put you in trouble with the law. On the other hand, an exhaust tip is relatively cheap (prices start at around $20) and easy to install, and worth the effort if you want a better-looking rear end, a more durable exhaust outlet, or a minor change in sound. Just don't expect it to deliver the performance and aural benefits of a proper aftermarket exhaust system.

Tech Report: How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.
  • Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.
  • It has been revealed that but access is only the first step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

It has been revealed that but access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

According to recent reports, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

According to recent reports, other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

As governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

Sources indicate that national electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

In 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

Recent findings suggest that ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

According to recent reports, in the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and initiative grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

In Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Industry observers note that being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

Even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

Industry observers note that in Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

In Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they plan and direct investment.

Rather than starting with how many new connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

According to recent reports, energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Sources indicate that courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat.

According to recent reports, your favorite same-day-delivery online superstore wants to give you gas. That's right: Amazon, the one-stop shop for furniture, groceries, health care, and household knickknacks, is now offering its Prime members an additional fuel-saving perk. Already in a fuel-savings friendship with energy company BP, Amazon is now doubling its daily discount to 20 cents off per gallon. But, of course, there's some fine print attached. The big bonus is exclusive to Amazon Prime members with active earnify account, only applies to one fill up every Friday, and lasts through January 2027.

The marketplace that Jeff Bezos built learned its lesson with standalone convenience stores, so instead of building gas stations or buying up existing chains, Amazon is letting BP handle the brick-and-mortar thing. BP's earnify rewards app was introduced in 2024 and now offers discounts at the pump and inside convenience stores.

The standard fuel discount for all earnify members is 5 cents off a gallon, but its partnership with Amazon, which started the same year earnify launched, allows Amazon Prime members to enjoy an everyday deal of 10 cents off per gallon every day and 20 cents on Fuel Up Fridays.

This isn't the first time Amazon has helped improve motorists' weekend vibes either. The last Fuel Up Fridays promo happened earlier this year and lasted from April 3 to May 29, and before that, the special ran from October 17 until December 26, 2025. Blame (or thank) the economy, but the current savings spree is going to last more than three months. Since October 2, Fuel Up Fridays has been up and running. If you're doing any winter holiday travels by RV, car, or truck, you're in luck because the Amazon-BP discount continues beyond the New Year. Although you can't always avoid dumb winter drivers, at least you know you can save 20 cents during fill-ups until January 29.

Industry observers note that you don't have to only stick with BP-branded gas stations for this special promotion, either. It applies to all BP and Amoco locations, as well as participating ampm and Thorntons stores. That means you have more than 7,500 pit stops across the U.S. to choose from.

Sources indicate that for the Amazon fuel deal, the sign-up process requires a one-time activation. Prime members can claim the gas discount via the Amazon Fuel page on a web browser or by scrolling through the Partner Offers section under the Prime category in the app. A caveat of the TGIF 20-cents-off bonus is that it can only be used only on one fill-up every Friday, and maxes out at 35 gallons. And given how BP is making a fortune drilling oil, giving back 10 cents on the gallon is the very least they can do.

Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, Volkswagen is marking the 50th anniversary of the GTI by showing how uncompromising an electric GTI with motorsport ambitions can be. The concept car will be presented to the public next week at the Essen Motor Show (27 November to 6 December 2026). Its performance figures meet a two-door silhouette and flared wings as well as a large front splitter, diffuser and rear wing. The result: a powerful appearance and maximum downforce for fast laps. At the same time, the concept vehicle provides a preview of how the GTI idea can be further developed in the electric age.

Sources indicate that kai Grünitz, Member of the Board of Management for Technical Development, Volkswagen Brand and Brand Group Core: “The GTI has been one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years. This year, we introduced our GTI as an electric vehicle in series production for the first time. With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, we are showing how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world. Our platform strategy and MEB+ give us the technological freedom to make even extreme concepts possible.”.

Designed for performance. The design of the newly introduced ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the production model, the 166 kW (226 PS) ID. Polo GTI. In both models, the drive power is transmitted to the front axle. In the 270 kW (367 PS) ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, this power delivery is controlled – thanks in part to an electronically regulated front differential lock (VAQ) – so that the model reaches 100 km/h from a standstill in just 4.7 seconds with Launch Control. Like the drive system, the electrical infrastructure has also been adapted to the high performance of the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept. The 52 kWh high-voltage battery can provide up to 290 kW at short notice, enabling a top speed of 240 km/h. The DCC (adaptive chassis control) has also been tuned for use on the racetrack and ensures precise handling and high traction in conjunction with the front differential lock. The new ceramic brakes of the one-box brake system are also designed for high performance.

According to recent reports, dynamics are visible in the design. On the exterior, the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept follows the powerful clarity of the ID. Polo GTI production model, while at the same time incorporating design elements that underline the motorsport characteristics. Particularly striking features are the two-door instead of four-door silhouette, pronounced flaring of the wings by 50 millimetres in each case, a large motorsport splitter at the front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser and a rear wing in carbon fibre that protrudes above the roof line.

Recent findings suggest that two-seater. Reduced to racing. The interior is also tailored to the racetrack, and only the basic layout of the overall cockpit has been adopted from the production model. This means there is no infotainment system, for example. The focus is solely on ergonomics and driving. The driver and front passenger sit on Recaro racing bucket seats with red 5-point harnesses. The rear and luggage compartment have been completely cleared. Instead of a rear seat system, a rollover bar painted in the GTI colour Tornado Red is integrated above and behind the front seats. The dash panel, side trims and many other details are covered in dark ArtVelours microfibre fabric with red topstitching – work that has been carried out with great precision by Volkswagen trainees. In many areas – in keeping with Volkswagen tradition – the young employees were directly involved in realisation of the concept vehicle by the Development department and designers.

550 instead of 290 newton-metres. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept features the high-torque APP550 motor. The special technical challenge here: this motor is actually intended for the rear of large models such as the ID. Tiguan or ID.7. It therefore had to be fitted into the smaller ID. Polo as front-wheel drive and additionally combined with an electronic front differential lock. Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management Volkswagen AG for Technology, and CEO of Volkswagen Group Components: “The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept indicates just how emotive electric mobility can be: This is made possible by our APP550, one of the most efficient electric drives in its class. Manufactured over one million times at the Group Components plant in Kassel, this drive was actually developed for larger vehicle classes. Integrating it into the Polo required millimetre precision and is a powerful example of engineering skill and teamwork at Volkswagen, from Development and Design through to our trainees who worked on the project.”.

It has been revealed that GTI from the master of modular platforms. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the modular electric drive (MEB+) platform with front-wheel drive. Volkswagen has used the basic technical layout of the production model and taken it to a new level of performance with a 104 kW (141 PS) more powerful electric drive. The result is the most dynamic interpretation of a front-wheel drive ID. model to date. At the other end of the scale is the Mission Efficiency, which is also based on the ID. Polo and set four world records as a particularly efficient near-production electric vehicle. Both concept vehicles show the large bandwidth offered by electric drive systems from maximum sportiness to outstanding efficiency.

2026 is the year of the GTI. Following the Golf GTI EDITION 50, the new ID.3 GTI (sales start early 2027) and the new ID. Polo GTI (available to order since October), the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is making its debut this year as the fourth new model under the umbrella of the iconic GTI product brand. No other compact sports car family has been as successful worldwide for half a century now – with more than 2.5 million units sold – as the GTI models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elle and Dakota Fanning have been in the spotlight for decades, but their upcoming project, “The Nightingale,” marks the first time they’ve played sisters onscreen—an experience that brought them “closer” together, both on set and at home.

While they’ve visited each other on set in the past and even separately played different versions of the same character in the 2001 film “I Am Sam,” Elle, 28, told Vanity Fair that actually working with each other is a totally different ball game.

In a recent development, “It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer,” she mentioned. “Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”.

Dakota, 32, confirmed that they took their mother’s advice.

It has been revealed that “We did really savor it,” she noted. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything. That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”.

That noted, the job wasn’t easy. The Fannings traveled to Budapest to shoot on location, where they lived together.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” mentioned Elle.

After a long day of using lots of “brain power” on set, the sisters had to find a way to “recharge” each evening.

For Dakota and Elle, that meant eating lots of Thai food and streaming “The Real Housewives,” true crime, and “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”—the TV series the younger sister stars in, which was released while they filmed “The Nightingale.”.

Dakota revealed that on a day off, she’d often find herself cleaning up after Elle, which was poetic as her character, Vianne, also tidies her sister Isabelle’s mess.

According to recent reports, “Her bed in the mornings is like a tornado has run through it,” she mentioned. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”.

The older sister said that “it became a routine,” and she “always made her bed like that” when possible.

Elle stated, “It’s art imitating life, because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed, too.”.

Dakota and Elle were born in Conyers, GA. As young girls, they traveled between the Atlanta suburb and Los Angeles to work before relocating to the West Coast full time.

“When we were younger, we wanted to make sure that people saw us differently, and we wanted to give each other space to carve our own path,” Elle told Vanity Fair in 2025. “But as adults, it’s been very fulfilling to merge.”.

One of the most major ways the sisters have merged their lives in adulthood was in 2017, when they purchased a gorgeous $2.3 million property together.

According to Architectural Digest, they lived in a Cape Cod-style home in the Valley Village area of San Fernando Valley.

The 4,550-square-foot residence was perched at the end of a private, gated driveway and had a very classic aesthetic with white rose bushes planted along the front walkway.

The interiors were defined by delicate details, such as baby blue brocade-patterned walls, intricate chandeliers, and coffered ceilings.

The sisters sold the six-bedroom, six-bathroom estate for just under $2.7 million in May 2020.

It’s clear that Dakota was a fan of the dwelling’s traditional style, as she bought a very similar-looking home in Toluca Lake for $2.95 million in 2019, just before offloading the property she shared with Elle.

Solar module manufacturer Thornova Solar and Nextpower, a provider of advanced solar tracker and structural solutions, marked a milestone in their growing strategic cooperation with the signing of a Master Supply Agreement (MSA).

The agreement, revealed at RE+ 2026, further strengthens the collaboration between the two companies, combining Thornova Solar’s U.S.-made solar modules with Nextpower’s U.S.-manufactured steel frame technology. The expanded effort is designed to deliver increased domestic content opportunities and enhanced structural performance, providing greater value to customers developing utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects across the United States.

According to the companies, integrating advanced steel frame solutions into selected Thornova Solar module series addresses two increasingly notable priorities in the U.S. solar market: maximizing domestic content and improving module resilience under demanding environmental conditions.

The combined solution offers several key benefits:.

The solution is particularly relevant for projects in demanding U.S. environments, including high-wind regions across the Midwest and Southeast, where structural reliability and long-term module performance are critical considerations.

“The signing of this Master Supply Agreement represents an crucial step in strengthening our relationship with Nextpower and expanding the value we deliver to U.S. customers,” noted Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director of Thornova Solar. “By bringing together U.S.-made solar modules and domestically manufactured steel frame technology, we are helping our customers increase domestic content while benefiting from stronger, more resilient module solutions. This is exactly the kind of collaboration needed to advance a competitive U.S. solar manufacturing ecosystem.”.

In a recent development, “We’re excited to deepen our strategic collaboration with Thornova and bring modules featuring Nextpower’s domestically manufactured steel frames to the U.S. market,” said Jenya Meydbray, vice president and general manager of Nextpower. “NX CoreFrame offers a significant opportunity to advance module strength and reliability, addressing industry challenges such as glass breakage and demanding environmental loads while delivering greater confidence to solar developers and owners.”.

The MSA reflects the shared commitment of both companies to strengthening domestic manufacturing and delivering solutions that respond to the evolving technical and commercial requirements of the U.S. solar market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as the average latest car price hits unrealistic highs, it only furthers the case for affordable vehicles. To provide some respite for desperate consumers, the Slate Truck no one can seem to stop talking about is coming soon in the U.S., and Italy's friendly but limited Fiat Topolino is breaching America's shores as well. The French, too, have come up with their own little practical, affordable utility EV, although this one is not coming to America. It's called La Bagnole. Points to the brand, Kilow, for the name, which translated to English is actually "the car.".

In a recent development, at first glance the little EV looks as if a Jeep and kei truck had a dependable, indestructible love child — indestructible simply because it's French. With the unrealistic expectations established in the "Carnage A Trois" episode of "The Grand Tour," where the trio tested the resilience of French cars in the "French way," by association these cars could be impossible to destroy, no?

According to recent reports, the beauty of it is, if La Bagnole is a little destructible and breaks, Kilow has designed repairs to be simple. And even the batteries can be fixed, as they house individually replaceable cells.

The tiny tank of an EV truck is built on a steel chassis, with a customizable body. Customers can opt to have a removable roof color-matched to the body or go one further and also add transparent doors. Either choice allows the addition of optional roofbars for extra hauling ability. At the rear, flooring and tailgate can be Kilow's resinated wood fiber, which doesn't require any extra maintenance, while the Okoumé wood option does require the occasional varnishing. It also comes in at an extra 990 euros (about $1,100). If you prefer a more van-like delivery car look, there's a covered tailgate option as well.

In a recent development, kilow markets La Bagnole as a simple vehicle. There are not a lot of parts to it, including no heating or cooling controls. What you can get is a minimalist dashboard made of the same resinated wood fiber or the Okoumé wood as well, fitted with a screen for battery updates, as well as toggle switches for the horn, wipers, washer fluid, and lights. You can really go all out and get a phone holder so you have your own navigation and tunes at the ready. No need to 3D-print it like you would have to for a Slate Truck.

It has been revealed that the vehicle's less simple side comes down to the color choices, of which there are 24. Twelve are solid colors, including quite the array across the rainbow, except for red and purple. Six gradient choices transition between two colors, and then there are the flecked colors reminiscent of a granite countertop, showing up as "Memories" on a page translated from French to English. Match those to steel or alloy rims, and mud guards for a polished look.

Power for La Bagnole is available in three battery capacities and ranges. Unlicensed drivers in France, likely more in city regions, can purchase two kinds of 28 mph batteries. The smaller of them is 6 kWh with a range of 43.5 miles, and the Long Range is a 12 kWh battery good for 102 miles. Licensed drivers can buy a 12 kWh battery with that same 102-mile range, but with a top speed of 50 mph. Charging can be done from a 220V household outlet, which Kilow claims will take about three to five hours for a full charge, depending on the size of the battery.

In a recent development, the accessories are fun as well. Avid campers can order a rooftop tent made by Decathlon, as long as you select a hardtop option. And if you about double the price of the tent, you can also get the camping kit complete with essential items like mugs, a coffee maker, stove and cooking pots, with the most attractive additions of the kit being the pressurized cooler, and pressurized shower. For the business-minded folks, you can also get your manufacturer logo added to the side panels, tailgate, and even the hardtop.

In a recent development, each build takes about three months to complete, with prices ranging from 10,800 to 13,690 euros, which also includes the value-added tax (VAT). That's approximately $11,913 to $15,101 in the U.S. Yet as is the case for many fun vehicles made abroad, Americans will not be getting these little trucks as Kilow focuses sales on France and Europe. If we were to ever land these in the future, though, there could certainly be a case for using these utilitarian cuties across a good part of the country.

Courts Are Undecided As To Whether Police Need Warrants For Flock Camera Data

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the operative word in this story's headline is "undecided." Because whether a police officer needs a warrant to use data obtained via Flock cameras seems to fall across multiple legalistic gray areas that aren't settled law.
  • In a recent development, just for background (if you've been living in some paradise lacking this technology), Flock is a brand of device known as an automated license plate reader, or ALPR.
  • According to recent reports, in the past we've reported on Flock cameras violating highway safety standards as well as the Fourth Amendment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the operative word in this story's headline is "undecided." Because whether a police officer needs a warrant to use data obtained via Flock cameras seems to fall across multiple legalistic gray areas that aren't settled law. Funny that our nation's founders didn't anticipate technology that surveils every driver (of course, they didn't anticipate cars, either).

In a recent development, just for background (if you've been living in some paradise lacking this technology), Flock is a brand of device known as an automated license plate reader, or ALPR. And Flock contracts with law enforcement agencies across the country. Those agencies can opt to share their data with other police departments across a region, state, or the entire United States. In turn, that means police in many jurisdictions can use Flock to track anyone's movements nationally.

According to recent reports, in the past we've reported on Flock cameras violating highway safety standards as well as the Fourth Amendment. But the meat of that latter nugget, of cops needing a warrant to obtain Flock camera data — or not needing a warrant — and whether that violates the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, is still up in the air.

Recent findings suggest that in case you're fuzzy on the law, the Fourth Amendment protects all of us against unreasonable searches and seizures. It requires law enforcement to have probable cause (i.e., reason to suspect a crime) in order to pull us over, search our cars, and fine or arrest us. The nub of this debate has  been addressed recently by judges in two states, and they've issued contradictory rulings about this very question: Do police need a warrant or don't they?

Last month, at a federal district court in northern Oklahoma, Judge Sara Hill ruled that a Tulsa sheriff's deputy violated a defendant's Fourth Amendment rights when he used Flock's database to conduct a nationwide search on a Mazda SUV's previous location. The result: Pulling over 50 sightings from ALPRs across the U.S., he could see everywhere the car had been for the past 30 days.

But according to the ruling, the only reason for the officer's initial suspicion was that the Mazda SUV was from California. The officer followed the Mazda, noted a few driving infractions including following another car on the highway too closely, and pulled over the driver, Melissa Kyle. The traffic stop resulted in a search of Kyle's car, which led to Kyle's arrest on a charge of possession of marijuana. However, the charge was thrown out when Hill ruled that the officer's search of Flock data was unlawful and required a warrant. And so any evidence found subsequently was inadmissible.

And yet a week later, an Ohio county judge ruled in an entirely opposite manner. Judge John Vavra of Belmont County Common Pleas Court ruled that a driver doesn't have a right to privacy that would restrict the use of Flock camera data.

Sources indicate that just to be clear, the federal court ruling is far more likely to lead to constitutional debate than a lower-level county case in Ohio. Court watchers say Hill's ruling is consistent with how the Supreme Court has declared certain mass-surveillance tech unconstitutional. And it's worth unpacking what happened in Oklahoma, because it illustrates how a police officer — with access to data via Flock — jumped to a conclusion that the judge in that case says violates the Fourth Amendment.

Sources indicate that in 2022, we reported that Flock cameras could be used to track people traveling across state lines for abortion services. Then earlier this year 404 Media reported that cops in Texas did exactly that, tracking a woman via ALPR for seeking a legal abortion in another state.

Sources indicate that the point of raising that matter is that the police didn't have a warrant for that ALPR search. The officer in Oklahoma also didn't have a warrant to search the movement of a car with California plates. The officer told Kyle that her long trip to and from California, spending only a little time there, had made him dubious about her — something he only knew about via Flock. Judge Hill found that the officer's logic didn't pass the test of reasonable suspicion and that, crucially, he decided to detain Kyle before he discovered that she had marijuana (recreational pot is illegal in Oklahoma).

Judge Hill ruled that the ALPR "... search was not supported by probable cause, and it was done without a warrant in violation of Kyle's Fourth Amendment rights." Hill found that ALPRs constitute "dragnet-style surveillance," and that "it becomes constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts ... and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.".

We don't know whether Hill's ruling will carry up to higher courts. But this feels like the Fourth Amendment wreaking its own kind of vengeance. Especially because police have used Flock technology to stalk ex-partners, retaliate against police critics, racially profile minorities, and surveil protestors. Not to mention looking stuff up on Flock using search terms like LMAO. We're just journalists, not judges, but LMAO doesn't seem like probable cause. Nor does pulling the travel records of any car with out-of-state plates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that JJA ESS has debuted its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations.
  • According to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service.
  • A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that JJA ESS has debuted its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving the team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions, and future updates.

According to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.

A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the data record to the battery, enabling access to information throughout its entire lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, CO₂ footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, condition, supply chain due diligence, and end-of-life disposal. Taken together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification to the end of the product lifecycle.

According to recent reports, for manufacturers, the challenge lies not simply in creating a QR code. The data must be traceable back to its source, up-to-date, and accessible in accordance with regulatory and business requirements. Companies must also manage access to sensitive information and comply with regulations governing cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is particularly relevant for companies operating in multiple markets. When companies utilize a third-party platform, its functionality, access to data fields, and interoperability can be determined by the provider’s configuration and service model.

In a recent development, JA ESS developed the platform internally and hosts it in its own cloud environment. Data policies, access permissions, and future platform updates are managed by the JA ESS internal team. This team ensures compliance with EU regulations regarding data access, presentation, and updates, while also giving JA ESS greater control over data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements change and real-world applications provide further insights.

In a recent development, JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the JA brand. As a central component of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS offers a wide range of FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent, and customized solutions for the large-scale, commercial, and industrial sectors as well as the residential market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four months after announcing their split, “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” cast member Angie Katsanevas and her estranged husband, Shawn Trujillo, are now living in separate homes.

“Recently, Shawn has bought a place that’s two minutes down the street. And I’m at home with Elektra,” Katsanevas revealed in a new People magazine interview.

According to a Page Six report, Trujillo's latest pad is a $1.1 million condo he purchased in September. The two-story dwelling spans 2,568 square feet and includes three bedrooms and 4.5 bathrooms.

The couple, who married in June 1999, have yet to legally divorce, but are "moving toward" that status.

“We are separated. We haven’t put it on paper, but we are not reconciling as far as staying married,” the reality TV star, 53, explained. “I hate the major D-word, but I’ll just have to say that, yeah, we are moving toward the big D.”.

The salon owner’s home—which viewers will recognize from the reality series—is a sprawling hillside estate that has been on and off the market for the past two years.

Industry observers note that the four-bedroom, three-bathroom modern abode was first listed for $4.5 million in September 2024. The price was decreased to $4.38 million in March 2025, then to $3.85 million just two months later.

It has been revealed that by December of last year, the listing was removed. It hit the market again in January 2026 for $3.85 million, where it sat for most of the year before being removed on Oct. 14.

Recent findings suggest that the couple purchased the 6,369-square-foot residence for an undisclosed sum in 2020. With soaring ceilings, white ash floors, and lots of sleek, marble surfaces, the modern abode has a distinct luxurious aesthetic.

Sources indicate that the home has two primary suites, with one that includes a fireplace, sitting area, and double-vanity bathroom with a striking view of the surrounding Utah landscape. There are also dual walk-in closets.

The second is located on the main floor and also has two-walk in closets and a gorgeous bathroom.

Features in pairs seem to be a feature of the home in general, as there are also two kitchens. In addition to the chic white minimalist space at the center of the home, a concealed catering kitchen is equipped with Miele appliances, a separate refrigerator and freezer, and a space for staff to prepare food.

Recent findings suggest that it seems as if, despite the separation, daily life hasn’t changed too much in the home. Katsanevas noted that Trujillo stops by most days to pick up their 15-year-old daughter, Elektra, and take her to school.

Industry observers note that “He’ll come in and have coffee,” she explained. “He’ll bring her home from lessons, and we’ll have dinner together. We are still just spending time together. We’re best friends. We are peaceful, it’s positive. We have a lot to do together.”.

She noted that Trujillo remains close with her father and will celebrate the holidays with the family.

“My dad sends him all of his favorite dishes and continues to cook for him,” noted Katsanevas. “Shawn will spend Thanksgiving and Christmas with my family.”.

Although they are still connected in many ways, Katsanevas noted that after nearly three decades together, “space and doing things independently” have brought clarity.

Industry observers note that “We are even going to different churches now,” she shared. “And that’s huge for me. We started out going to the same church.”.

Katsanevas also shut down rumors that she had initiated the split over their opposing political stances, a rumor that started after she cited their “different views” in a confessional interview during a recent episode of “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”.

Industry observers note that “I’m not throwing a 30-year marriage away because of rumors or political views,” she mentioned. “There are so many things that Shawn and I have grown apart and have different views on, a lot of things at this stage of life. And it’s not one thing. It’s just, we’re very different people.”.

They’re still business partners, however, and are set to open a new hair salon together in Miami.

“We are continuing to grow our brand together, even though we are separated,” she noted.

Katsanevas and Trujillo presently operate nine locations of their business, Lunatic Fringe Salon, across Utah, Ohio, and Idaho.

While she’s focused on remaining positive, Katsanevas said it took some time to work through the complicated feelings that accompanied the change.

Recent findings suggest that “It does take a minute to mourn the loss of the way your life once was and what it looked like,” she said. “I’ve processed, I’ve cried, I’ve accepted. I’ve had to swim away from the muddy waters to get to the clear water and say, ‘OK, I’m coming out of this and I’m going to be OK.’”.

Tech Report: Ranking Today's 4 Main V12 Supercars By Horsepower As They Scream Into The Sunset

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that since burning tons of fuel to move one, maybe two, people around isn't the greatest thing for the planet, massive V12 engines are a dying breed.
  • And for the supercar geeks about to run to the comments to point out that one McLaren F1-shaped omission, Gordon Murray's T.50 did indeed use a V12 — a naturally aspirated 3.9-liter developed by Cosworth, no less — but that car actually ended production back in the summer of 2025, so it's out of the running.
  • Despite ranking at the bottom in terms of power, the Ferrari 12Cilindri is arguably, for one obvious reason, the car most overtly proud of the fact that it still uses a V12 — that name, by the way, is pronounced "dodici cilindri," where the first c is a "ch" sound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that since burning tons of fuel to move one, maybe two, people around isn't the greatest thing for the planet, massive V12 engines are a dying breed. Even among supercars, there are pretty much only four left that use what is arguably the most romantic engine layout possible. You can count 'em on one hand: there's a Ferrari, a Lamborghini, an Aston Martin, and a Pagani. If you're curious as to how they rank purely in terms of horsepower, you've come to the right place.

And for the supercar geeks about to run to the comments to point out that one McLaren F1-shaped omission, Gordon Murray's T.50 did indeed use a V12 — a naturally aspirated 3.9-liter developed by Cosworth, no less — but that car actually ended production back in the summer of 2025, so it's out of the running. In a similar vein, the Aston Martin Valkyrie indeed made enough power to sit atop this list, but production stopped back in 2024. Without further ado, then, here are today's four main V12 supercars, ranked by horsepower.

Despite ranking at the bottom in terms of power, the Ferrari 12Cilindri is arguably, for one obvious reason, the car most overtly proud of the fact that it still uses a V12 — that name, by the way, is pronounced "dodici cilindri," where the first c is a "ch" sound. The cilindris in question are inside a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12 making 819 hp. The 12Cilindri can go from zero to 62 mph in 2.9 seconds and has a top speed exceeding 211 mph. While mighty by any standard, forward thrust plays second fiddle to this engine's real allure: a sky-high redline of 9,500 rpm.

In regular form, those revs generate power going to the rear axle through an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission. The recent big news about this car, however, is the introduction of a Manuale variant that pairs that V12 with a gated "manual" transmission that is, in reality, a meticulously programmed simulation of a three-pedal gearbox. There's been much debate over whether the Manuale's authenticity matters, but I'm just glad its screaming V12 remains a genuine article.

Besting its Ferrari rival by precisely 5 hp is the Aston Martin Vanquish. Where the 12Cilindri is staunchly naturally aspirated, the Aston makes its power with forced induction, adding two turbos to its 5.2-liter V12 to make 824 horses. Zero to 60 mph is achieved in 3.2 seconds, and it'll hit a top speed of 214 mph.

Industry observers note that it's a real Aston engine, too, because unlike the Mercedes V8s you find in the brand's modern Vantage and DBX, this V12 is a continuation of the in-house motor that powered the old DB11 and DBS Superleggera. In addition to stronger connecting rods, higher flow-rate fuel injectors, and quicker turbos, this motor gets a latest Boost Reserve function that builds boost in the background during partial throttle so it's ready to go when you do floor it. I've driven it, and in practice, the Vanquish pulls off the Aston Martin thing of being just as exciting as a sporting machine as it is livable and comfortable as a GT car.

Sources indicate that like any good exotic automaker, Aston loves a good limited-run special model, and, for posterity, the Vanquish-based Valen takes this engine and makes a slightly nuttier 838 hp. There's also a 705-hp, manual-transmission Valour, plus a more track-focused, 735-hp variant called the Valiant. As if being a manual V12 Aston made for the track wasn't cool enough, that last one happened to come about as a personal commission from two-time world champ and Aston Martin Formula 1 driver, Fernando Alonso.

When it comes to pure horsepower, none of Aston's current V12 fare beats the Pagani Utopia. An exotic among exotics, the Utopia is powered by a twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V12, made just for this car by Mercedes-AMG, pumping out a mighty 864 hp.

Sources indicate that you can get the Utopia with a seven-speed automated manual gearbox, but I'm not sure why you would when the seven-speed actual manual is right there. In true Pagani fashion, it has a gated gearbox where the entire shift linkage is exposed and shiny and glorious. Zero to 60 mph is remarked to take around 3.0 seconds, and the Roadster is electronically limited to 217 mph, but tellingly, a lot of Pagani's own literature shies away from discussing such specs.

This is not a car that seems to concern itself much with instrumented testing — you wouldn't strap a stopwatch to the Mona Lisa, now would you? To put it another way: the Pagani Utopia is arguably the car on this list I'd be in the most awe of coming across in the wild, and that insane 864-hp V12 somehow isn't even in the top three reasons that's the case.

If technical dominance is what you're after, the most powerful V12 supercar on the market today is the Lamborghini Revuelto SV, which makes 1,050 horsepower. Mind you, that doesn't come solely from its naturally aspirated 6.5-liter V12. Instead, it's a culmination of that engine plus three hybrid electric motors — yep, in case you missed the memo, both of Lamborghini's supercars are now plug-in hybrids.

Sources indicate that in a parallel universe where the Revuelto wasn't a hybrid, however, it'd come last on this list because its V12 alone produces "just" 814 hp, six fewer ponies than that equally large Ferrari motor. But that's not how the game is played.

Industry observers note that taken as a whole, the electrified Lambo gets from zero to 62 mph in just 2.4 seconds, notably quicker than every other car here, and it reaches a top speed of 216 mph. The fastest and most powerful production Lamborghini ever dominates on a dragstrip not just on the back of its immense horsepower but also because it's the only car on this list with all-wheel-drive. Each front wheel is powered by a dedicated electric motor (the remaining e-motor is at the back, helping out that V12).

Sources indicate that as it happens, I was fortunate enough to drive a "regular," non-SV Revuelto last year, which made a relatively paltry 1,001 hp. The speed was, in a word, ridiculous, and that V12 soundtrack remains an absolute treat. In the admittedly small pantheon of V12 supercars that remain, the Ferrari may be more pure, the Aston more refined, and the Pagani more special, but in the contest of pure horsepower and speed, the Lamborghini Revuelto, for now at least, sits at the peak.

Recent findings suggest that ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin believes younger generations investing in stocks and digital assets instead of housing could help ease pressure on property prices. However, he notes crypto still needs something that makes housing attractive: stability.

In a recent development, buterin thinks that housing creates incentives for owners to keep property prices high, even when cheaper homes would benefit society. Digital assets could offer an alternative, but today’s platforms often encourage excessive speculation.

“We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets,” Buterin wrote on X.

It has been revealed that his comments raise a question for Ethereum. Can the network evolve beyond speculative trading and become dependable infrastructure for people building long-term digital wealth?

One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities.That….

According to recent reports, ethereum’s development roadmap increasingly focuses on making the network faster, more efficient, and harder to disrupt. Its next major upgrade, Glamsterdam, is in testing, and ethereum.org lists a mainnet launch for Q4 2026 with no date confirmed yet. The upgrade introduces several changes designed to improve Ethereum’s capacity without sacrificing decentralization.

One major feature is Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS). It moves the relationship between block proposers and builders directly into Ethereum’s protocol, reducing reliance on external relays and additional trust assumptions.

Industry observers note that another important development is Block-Level Access Lists. The feature prepares Ethereum to process unrelated transactions in parallel rather than handling everything sequentially.

It has been revealed that these improvements could help Ethereum support more financial applications while keeping its infrastructure accessible to independent node operators. So, if digital assets are expected to become long-term financial instruments rather than vehicles for short-term speculation, this is very much needed.

Ethereum also provides an established foundation for staking, stablecoins, decentralized lending, and tokenized real-world assets. These applications could give investors more ways to hold and use digital wealth without constantly trading volatile tokens.

Yet, security, reliable applications, and responsible financial products must develop alongside network capacity.

Recent findings suggest that ethereum’s market performance presents a contrasting picture. ETH is trading just a notch above $1,800. This leaves the coin 63% below its all-time high of $4,946. The decline highlights the gap between Ethereum’s technological ambitions and its current market valuation.

Ethereum’s network utility and ETH’s investment performance are also not interchangeable. More applications and transactions can strengthen the ecosystem, but they do not create proportional demand for ETH.

The token still plays an key role as Ethereum’s native transaction currency, staking asset, and collateral across decentralized finance. For this reason, continued growth in staking, stablecoins, and tokenized assets could strengthen ETH’s underlying investment narrative.

Buterin’s comments are bigger than a debate about housing affordability. He is effectively challenging the crypto industry to build assets and platforms that encourage long-term ownership rather than constant speculation.

Ethereum has several pieces of that foundation already, including proof-of-stake security, smart contracts, and an expanding financial ecosystem.

Its upcoming upgrades aim to improve the infrastructure supporting those applications. But the network still needs to prove that its technology can deliver dependable financial products at scale.

Maybe Don't Paint Your Car With House Paint

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (335 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the mates at Australia's creative Garbage Time have done it again.
  • Recent findings suggest that you may be surprised to hear this, but no — covering a house-painted car in dust, dirt, pollen, and bird droppings does not, in fact, improve the quality of the paint.
  • According to recent reports, after a year of dealing with outdoor conditions, the Corolla's paint is pretty thoroughly wrecked, which is saying something for a carmaker noted for its terrible colors.

Sources indicate that the mates at Australia's creative Garbage Time have done it again. Last year they painted a Toyota Corolla entirely with house paint, more or less color matched to the car's existing paint by a local hardware store chain. This turned out to be a bad idea, as house paint is fundamentally very different from your favorite automotive paints, but then the geniuses behind the channel had a brain blast: Leave the car outside, parked under a tree, for a year. Surely that would make things better, right?

Recent findings suggest that you may be surprised to hear this, but no — covering a house-painted car in dust, dirt, pollen, and bird droppings does not, in fact, improve the quality of the paint. Washing it afterward doesn't help, either, because a touchless wash can't really get anything out of that soft, ductile paint. No, once you've covered your car in hardware-store house paint — without any preparation, primer, or clear coat — you're pretty much screwed.

According to recent reports, after a year of dealing with outdoor conditions, the Corolla's paint is pretty thoroughly wrecked, which is saying something for a carmaker noted for its terrible colors. A touchless wash did absolutely nothing to fix that, and even a hand wash was only a marginal improvement. The house paint, constantly referred to as "gummy" throughout the video, is just too good at grabbing onto dirt and holding onto it. It's also pretty great at peeling off the car when aggressively cleaned.

In a recent development, from a distance, the house-painted Corolla actually doesn't look terrible — a bit wet, like the paint isn't fully dry, but not uncannily so. It's clearly not a factory paint job, but from 20 feet away you'd be hard-pressed to tell this automotive travesty from a poor rattlecan job that combined proper materials with improper technique. This Corolla got neither the right stuff nor the right methods. But hey, at least it was cheap.
