#76418. 8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2105 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

8 Things Your iPhone Does As You Flip Your Car Down An Embankment

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there.
  • It has been revealed that apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later).
  • It's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A phone puts in a lot of work while we're driving around, especially if your car's infotainment system is painfully old and it's doing double duty there. And while plenty has been said about how our phones can help cause a crash – texting-while-driving bans exist in every state but one – we don't talk as much about how they can be downright heroic when one actually occurs.

It has been revealed that apple introduced Crash Detection with the iPhone 14 in 2022 (it works on iPhone 14 or later running iOS 16 or later). The underlying technology unlocks a number of possibilities, some of which could literally save a user's life. That's because once your phone knows you've been in a crash, it can do a number of phone-based tasks that you might no longer be in a position to do yourself, from calling 911 and letting them know where to find you to alerting your emergency contacts that something has gone awry.

It's worth noting that nothing here is exclusive to Apple. In fact, Google Pixel phones have been doing crash detection since 2019. But since more Americans use iPhones than every other competing device combined, getting Crash Detection into iOS represented the first mainstream on-by-default introduction of the technology in the United States, even if many owners were unaware it was even there. So if you have a different device, there's a chance it can do what's being discussed today. We're sharing the iPhone perspective for the sake of being relevant to the most users and letting us be specific about the details. So here's what your phone might get up to right after you overcorrect from hitting inexplicable gravel on that backroad sweeper.

According to recent reports, your iPhone starts determining that you're in a crash based on a bunch of real-time data that it's taking in all the time — think change in speed, impact force, and even changes in air pressure. But before it takes any action that could lead to a rescue helicopter being summoned to your location or scaring the daylights out of your emergency contact, it's going to evaluate whether you've actually been traveling along in a car versus, say, knocking your phone off a balcony or falling down a flight of stairs.

Recent findings suggest that there are no exact criteria that answer this question. A crash detection algorithm notes things like whether you are connected to a vehicle via Bluetooth, how rapidly it is passing through the range of nearby Wi-Fi connections, and even analyzes ambient engine sounds or road noise. The goal is to cobble together a clear enough picture of what's going on to distinguish between a phone being dropped on a moving subway and one flying through the air in an auto accident. It's an approach that had to be dialed in. When the feature was first introduced, there was a tendency for crash detection to be triggered in non-crash events, such as violent jostling on a roller coaster. Subsequent updates refined the criteria, aiming to reduce false positives and emergency crews being dispatched to amusement parks.

Apple has done research with crash labs to effectively draw this line, both determining when someone is traveling in a car and also filtering out minor incidents like a small fender bender or a phone simply being knocked on the floor while a vehicle is in motion.

Once your iPhone has established that you're likely traveling in a vehicle and not bungee jumping or getting your clock cleaned playing football, it uses on-device hardware to get a handle on how much trauma the laws of physics are putting on the phone and, by extension, probably you.

Sources indicate that newly introduced motion sensors introduced with the iPhone 14 include a three-axis gyroscope and high-g force accelerometer able to detect up to 256 Gs of force, which helps estimate if whatever is happening to you would land in a sufficiently severe place on something called the Maximum Abbreviated Injury Scale (MAIS). Apple notes it has set the crash detection threshold in an effort to detect incidents with a MAIS level 3 and higher, at which point your injuries are likely to include "major lacerations, multiple fractures, crushed limbs, and bruised organs." Like we said: not a fender bender.

Sources indicate that these sensors fire off more than 3,000 times per second, slowing your terrifying automotive mishap into a veritable eternity of data that captures the initial impact and every twist, turn, bump, and smash that follows. On the plus side, in this case your phone probably isn't spreading your information to advertisers, so there's that.

Sources indicate that in addition to cutting-edge tech like the gyroscope and accelerometer, the iPhone also leans on pre-existing hardware to decide if the thing you're experiencing is indeed a crash that warrants an emergency response. One of those is the microphone, which can capture the acoustic data needed to identify crash sounds and help distinguish a real crash from false alarms G-force data might trigger.

Sources indicate that perhaps even more unexpected than your phone listening for tire-screeching and tree-hitting sounds is what's going on with its internal barometer, a sensor used primarily to measure elevation changes for activity tracking and support location services. Because airbags have a lot more going on than you might think and can temporarily alter the ambient air pressure inside the car when they go off, that barometer can often recognize the clue and relay the data point to the algorithm for consideration.

In a recent development, none of this is a sure thing. If your windows are down, the barometer might not be able to detect the change in pressure and the sounds of the accident may or may not align with what Apple's programming has decided a crash sounds like. Similar to the logic that determined you were in a car in the first place, it takes a number of differently-weighted data points to come up with an educated assessment of the situation. That assessment may be wrong, in either direction.

And because all these calculations can be wrong in either direction, the iPhone does provide a couple of clear opportunities for you to indicate there's been a wacky misunderstanding rather than a dangerous crash before it mobilizes a dramatic and potentially expensive emergency response on your behalf.

Before springing into action, it'll first sound an audible alarm and show an alert on the screen. This lasts 10 seconds. If you swipe where indicated it will call emergency services and if you dismiss the alert it'll cancel the whole thing. Of course, emergencies being emergencies, you might not be able to do either, in which case a 30-second countdown will occur before it moves forward.

During this time your phone will be making loud noises you probably haven't heard before, vibrating in a way you didn't realize it was capable of, and activating an LED strobe. If you swipe to call emergency services, you'll be connected. If you take no action, presumably because you can't, not because you didn't notice the air raid warnings coming from your phone, the countdown reaches zero and the phone springs into action on your behalf.

If you didn't have the foresight to sail your car into a ravine someplace with respectable cell phone coverage, you might think that all of this would just result in you having to listen to your phone make awful noises while you try to get yourself out of a dangerous situation with a cheap seatbelt cutter tool followed by it realizing it doesn't have any service anyway.

Not so! Since 2022, iPhone users in the U.S. and Canada with iPhone 14 models and later have had access to Emergency SOS via satellite. Whether you swiped right during the scary countdown or allowed it to reach zero while unresponsive or otherwise indisposed, the phone can use a data connection via satellite to reach help if cell service isn't available. If you're in a position to operate the phone, this won't be a voice call. You start with an emergency text, which will connect to emergency services after you enter "Report Emergency" mode. This prompts you to describe your situation using multiple choice questions to narrow down your predicament and relay the appropriate information.

Depending on where you are, a satellite connection may or may not be readily available. Dense tree cover above or the fact that you're upside down under a car may limit your phone's ability to reach a satellite. If that turns out to be an concern, the screen will walk you through how to best get a connection, such as moving to a place with a clear view of the horizon, which hopefully you'll be in a position to do. Of course, having to get yourself to the top of a hill remains preferable to having to get yourself to the nearest town.

Recent findings suggest that if you have cell service, none of that satellite business happens. After you don't respond in time and the countdown reaches zero, the iPhone calls emergency services. Because you're presumably unavailable at this point, once emergency dispatch answers the call, they will hear a repeating audio message indicating that a serious car crash has been detected with an unresponsive person in need of help. The message also includes a search radius based on your approximate latitude and longitude.

Sources indicate that during this time, two-way audio is enabled and the repeating recording will play at a reduced volume, so if you become able to speak with emergency services or someone else arrives on the scene, the conversation can proceed like any other 911 call. The phone screen will be commandeered with a "Crash Detected" message and the available interface will include one button to stop replaying the recorded message and another to end the call.

By the way, this all works over Wi-Fi calling as well, so you've also got options if you happen to flip your car down an embankment and into a Starbucks or something.

According to recent reports, after your phone is done contacting emergency services, it can also send a message to your designated emergency contacts, letting them know that a crash has been detected and that 911 has been called. It will include an approximate location. This will appear as a text message coming from you, and its content will make it immediately apparent that something significant is happening.

This only works if you've set your phone up for emergency contacts, which you do somewhat unintuitively through the Health app. Apple explains how to do it on its support page, and now is as good a time as any to get that taken care of if you haven't already. While you're in there, you can also enter any medical information that emergency responders might benefit from having, which they can access under your phone's Medical ID feature.

Don't assume that you've designated your emergency contact just because your phone seems to already know who your mom is and reminds you to call her on her birthday. You can add more than one — just make sure that whoever you put in there is someone you're willing to wake up in the middle of the night with a terrifying text message they can never unsee.

According to recent reports, one of the most key takeaways here has nothing to do with satellite technology or crash identification algorithms. Car crashes are chaotic, and even as your phone is processing data with mind-bending speed and preparing to summon help if you need it, the device itself may also be flying somewhere you aren't going to be able to get it. This doesn't just matter because an unsecured phone can become a projectile that hurts you or someone else. It's also important because something simple like placing a call is trivial while you're driving along but can become impossible in an emergency. And the remarkable thing is that, provided your phone survives and detects the crash, it can still call for help without you ever laying a finger on it.

Industry observers note that you might have no earthly idea where the phone went when you need it. The screen might be shattered and your pleas to Siri might be met with "Here's 'Help!' by The Beatles on Apple Music." Crash Detection isn't foolproof, it can't detect every wreck, and your phone might fall off your motorcycle and tell your family you crashed. On the other hand, it just might save the day.

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

Sources indicate that companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

According to recent reports, the numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data highlights. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

Industry observers note that san Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The organization provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

Sources indicate that customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Recent findings suggest that among companies focused on AI-generated speech, Upcoming York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The manufacturer is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

Industry observers note that voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

The sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean manufacturer behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram declared plans to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

It has been revealed that more recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Recent findings suggest that overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”.

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the manufacturer’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.
  • The Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range.
  • To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s initial public offering priced above expectations for its IPO on Thursday, with the manufacturer’s fully diluted valuation coming to roughly $1.494 trillion—more than the total residential real estate values in many entire states.

The Claude developer, which will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, priced at $83 a share, above the predicted $70 to $78 range. The manufacturer sold 980 million Class A shares, raising an initial $81 billion and shattering SpaceX’s $72 billion record.

To help better understand the massive $1.494 trillion price tag, Realtor.com® put the number in terms of real estate—and the statistics are shocking.

San Francisco is a longtime hot spot for tech giants. It saw the growth of Google and Facebook, and has now become the landing spot for Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI startups. The constant stream of tech wealth, combined with a limited number of desirable homes, has created a competitive market. San Francisco County has a median sales price of $1.6 million, and yet, Anthropic blows the entire market out of the water.

Sources indicate that the aggregate value of every home for sale in San Francisco is a mere $8.6 billion, a small fraction of Anthropic's new valuation. Indeed, the total value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metro is $1.37 trillion, according to the 2-25 American Community Survey. Anthropic’s valuation exceeds that by about $123 billion.

This trend is consistent in 391 metros out of 393.

The only two metros with more owner-occupied home value than Anthropic is worth are Newly introduced York City, at $3.26 trillion, and Los Angeles, at $2.64 trillion.

Furthermore, the AI giant’s valuation tops the owner-occupied home value in 46 out of the 50 states, as well as Washington, DC.

The value of all owner-occupied homes in the state of Newly introduced Jersey comes in at $1.44 trillion, just shy of Anthropic’s valuation.

Throughout the country, all owner-occupied homes are worth $43.6 trillion. Anthropic’s valuation equals about 3.4% of all owner-occupied housing wealth in the United States.

When it comes to homes on the market, Anthropic’s valuation stacks up high.

Across the U.S., about 1.18 million homes are for sale, listed for a combined $816 billion. Anthropic’s valuation could snap up every single one and still have $678 billion left.

Even without the first $1 trillion of the valuation, the remaining $494 billion could buy every home for sale in the 20 metros with the highest total listing value with billions to spare: about 372,000 homes listed at a combined $356 billion.

As Anthropic’s debut is discussed, the valuation may be rounded to $1.49 trillion, as it’s common for financial figures to be kept to one or two digits. However, that dropped digit in the $1.494 trillion figure is $4 billion. That rounding error alone is greater than the combined value of every owner-occupied home in Racine, WI, which total $3.97 billion.

In a recent development, that same $4 billion could buy every home for sale in Alaska: 2,196 listings worth $1.16 billion. For a change in scenery, it could then cover every home for sale on Kauai, the Kapa’a, Hawaii, market, which has 356 listings worth $925 million, and still have about $1.9 billion left to purchase all the homes for sale in the Boulder, CO, metro area.

It’s no wonder the AI boom is reshaping markets in tech hubs like Fresh York City and San Francisco, when the valuation of just one firm looms so high.

#76413. Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP).
  • Sources indicate that the plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets.
  • As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that earlier this week, Jackery unveiled a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP). The program starts with New York City apartment residents. I went to the RE+ in Las Vegas to meet with leaders from Jackery and Every Electric to learn more.

Sources indicate that the plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets. For the customer, the process is simple:.

That’s it. As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery. Over the 11-year rated lifespan, purchasing the battery could increase the total net payback, although the upfront cost would be a little higher.

It seems almost too simple and convenient for the customer. However, a lot of complex work and coordination is happening behind the scenes. The Jackery battery is in communication with Every Electric, who automates power management to charge when electricity demand is low and discharge to run the air conditioner when electricity demand is high. This kind of active demand response can go far beyond the typical TOU initiative to directly mitigate utility demand shifts. Every Electric monitors data for each battery. The demand response of the combined storage across thousands of individual batteries is aggregated and sold to the utility, in this case Con Edison. Then the benefits are divided up and distributed to customers based on their contributions. Over 2000 batteries were in the initial trial phase, with a larger scale rollout planned next year. I am already on the waitlist, along with over 15,000 other NYC households.

Industry observers note that because it does not feed electricity back into the grid, implementation is much simpler. No electrician needed. The system monitors the amount of energy being stored and deployed at the point of use with no need for user intervention. Unlike traditional demand response that turns off appliances, there is no inconvenience to the user. Thermostats do not need to be adjusted. Smart appliances are not needed. The battery simply provides power when grid demand is high, shaving off the peaks.

Sources indicate that you may still be asking “what’s the catch?” Currently, the system needs to coordinate a large number of relatively small batteries under the same utility to have enough combined capacity to sell to the utility. To start, it is only being offered in New York City, which sets the blueprint. In the initial application, the batteries will be used with 120V air conditioners, up to around 12,000 BTU. This is a common size for NYC apartments, letting one battery size serve a wide range of customers, simplifying initial rollout. It also offers clear return on investment based on how much electricity is used, when that electricity is used and when demand peaks for the utility. However, I wouldn’t expect it to stop there.

In a recent development, the batteries being used are led by the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. This battery has 2042 Wh of capacity and up to 2200 W of output with 4400 W of surge power. A total of three outlets are on the front panel, as well as two USB-C and a USB-A port. Due to the UPS function, the portable power station adds protection and would be ideal to plug in a computer or sensitive electronics, in addition to the air conditioner. Although the VPP is based on air conditioner use, using all the outlets can potentially add to the amount of load shifted by the VPP and, as a result, increase the amount of payback for the customer. Plugging in other forms of energy consumption could also extend the benefit beyond the times of year when the air conditioner is being used.

According to recent reports, at 40% smaller and 34% lighter than the previous generation model, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 weighs 39.5 lb. That’s less than a 5-gallon water cooler bottle but less bulky to carry. Due to the plug and play nature, people changing apartments within the city can easily take it with them at 13.2” x 10.4” x 11.5”. Multiple levels of safety protections and a ruggedized portable design using automotive-grade LFP batteries ensure safe operation even if apartment occupants bump into it.

That portability also contributes to the emergency preparedness capability of the battery. For the months of the year when the air conditioning isn’t running, the battery could provide backup power for a refrigerator in a power outage, for example. Of course, Jackery also offers batteries specifically for refrigerators. Those batteries are not a part of the initial program… yet.

This also gets to a limitation of the current program. To keep the program manageable as it scales up, only one size of battery in one use case is initially being offered. Right now, the biggest challenge is scaling up. Making it too complicated at the start would make scaling up more difficult. However, once the program reaches scale, more options can become available. Jackery also offers batteries with greater aesthetic appeal, like the slim FridgeGuard, which may be a better fit for the homes of some customers. As the program scales up, the applications have the potential to diversify.

It has been revealed that much of RE+ focused on supplying power and storage for data centers. While residential clean energy tax credits (25D) have been cut, data centers can still benefit from the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit that can add up with bonuses to cover half the cost of the project. With additional state and federal incentives piled on top, the majority of the cost of data center ESS can be covered by subsidies. With the heavily subsidized storage and large-scale contracts with the utility, data centers can access benefits not typically available to residential customers.

It has been revealed that however, the plug-in VPP changes the energy storage dynamic. People get credit for energy storage deployment at the point of use. AI technology, rather than just being a consumer of resources, is being used to automate the VPP system and let the benefits flow to more families. By starting with small window air conditioners, the system also tends to provide relief to people living in typically older apartments, rather than the sleek upcoming high rises with multi-million-dollar apartments.

Industry observers note that there is no need for home electrical upgrades. In fact, by taking some of the load off the circuit, the potential for my wife to trip the breaker from ironing in the living room while the TV and air conditioner are running on the same breaker is reduced. As the energy monitoring comes directly from the battery, it also isn’t dependent on smart meters.

For the system to have enough total capacity to sell to the utility, the plug-in VPP needs to connect thousands of batteries to provide multiple MWh of storage. This scale can easily be accomplished in urban areas. In addition, the value of the system will heavily depend on the local price of electricity and the variability in price. In NYC, electricity is significantly more expensive than in most of the US.

According to recent reports, upcoming York City apartments are a perfect starting place. While apartments tend to be far more energy efficient than detached houses and have lower net emissions overall, many of us living in apartments have traditionally felt a bit left out on clean tech. We don’t have roofs for rooftop panels. We typically do not have attached garages to place large permanent batteries or access to modify the electrical panel. If we do have the ability to make electrical modifications to the apartment, they can be prohibitively expensive in NYC. As such, a plug-in VPP is an exciting development for those of us living in apartments.

In a recent development, A plug-in VPP also makes the benefits of battery energy storage more accessible to urban areas. Often, there is not room for container-sized batteries. In places like Latest York City, the fire regulations are so strict, and the permitting is so complicated that large-scale BESS becomes exceedingly difficult to execute. Large-scale BESS, if approved, could take years to deploy.

In a recent development, according to NREL, the national average full installed price of utility scale BESS was $334/kWh of capacity in 2024, with hardware making up roughly two thirds of the total. However, the cost would undoubtedly be higher in NYC. For comparison, the discounted Explorer 2000 v2 in this program (which avoids retail markup) comes in at $318.32/kWh, with no added permitting or installation cost. That is also significantly less than the installed cost of many home batteries used in traditional VPPs, like Tesla Powerwall. Once delivered, it can be online within minutes.

Currently, plug-in VPP is the fastest, easiest and least expensive way to add battery capacity that shaves peak demand on urban grids in the US.

As high draw usage like air conditioning increases, more stress is placed on the grid. Transformer and other electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades can be expensive. Having storage at the point of use reduces the amount of electricity that needs to flow through the grid during peak periods. As plug-in VPP is deployed more broadly, the benefits will be experienced more broadly. And CO2 emissions can drop in the process.

While the benefits of the program are already attractive, the initial program may just be the tip of the iceberg. In New York City, buildings over 25,000 square feet must reduce their greenhouse gas emissions under Local Law 97 (LL97). This includes many apartment complexes and offices. The deployment of batteries at the point of use has the potential to reduce emissions.

While the current batteries and air conditioners in the program are 120V, Jackery also makes batteries that are 240V. For appliances that have intermittent use but high draw, like heat pumps, hot water heaters, ranges, etc., 240V connections are often needed to provide the necessary power. The electrification of applications that were previously run on gas or fuel oil can greatly reduce building emissions. But many apartment buildings do not have 240V outlets available. However, larger Jackery models can charge on 120V, accumulate charge and discharge at 240V for intermittent use. There is potential for batteries to support the higher voltage electrification without expensive electrical upgrades while also providing VPP benefit. The math would have to work out and it hasn’t happened yet. But the potential is clearly there.

Overall, the potential applications for this approach are massive. Already, I can see the potential to transform energy storage in NYC. In talking with Jackery and Every Electric, I started thinking about where the technology could go from here. Plug-in VPP could apply far beyond just New York City. However, that is for a follow-up article.

In a recent development, sure, the 2027 Chevy Express is the same as the 2026 model, which was the same as the 2025, which was the same as the 2024, and so on. But all joking aside, the Bowtie brand's body-on-frame van has only been riding on the same platform for about three decades. That's nothing compared to what Morgan did with its sports cars. Even the upcoming Morgan Supersport 400, the company's most powerful vintage-look roadster yet, maintains its flowing pontoon-style fenders, ash-wood body frame, and disdain for most modern technologies. Despite being the first Morgan to come with hands-free calling, the Supersport doesn't have a touchscreen — just a small and simple driver display with a trip computer and a digital speedometer. As for advanced driver-assistance systems, well, the car doesn't even have a rearview camera. It's exempt from most federal safety regulations due to its highly limited production numbers. The company produced approximately 35,000 steel-chassis cars before switching to a new platform, representing an average of roughly 417 cars per year.

Sources indicate that morgan's long-running steel chassis was likewise fairly old-fashioned. Essentially just a pair of Z-shaped steel rails connected to each other by five cross-members, the chassis rode on a basic leaf-spring suspension at the back and a sliding-pillar configuration up front. And the roots of that front suspension go back even further, as it was developed by Henry Frederick Stanley (HFS) Morgan in 1910.

In a recent development, just to be clear, Morgan actually started using aluminum chassis in 2000, when it introduced one for its relatively short-lived line of Aero cars — starting with the Aero 8, which also stands out as the first Morgan model with a BMW powertrain. However, other Morgans continued to ride on the steel setup through 2020.

Meanwhile, Morgan was ready to introduce its upcoming CX platform made from bonded aluminum. It first underpinned the 2019 Morgan Plus Six, which was named for its BMW-sourced I6 turbo engine. The lightweight chassis weighed a mere 220 pounds, but it was so stiff that the Plus Six had twice the torsional rigidity of the car it replaced in the Morgan lineup.

Then, in 2025, Morgan premiered the new Supersport with a further evolution of the CX chassis. The Supersport's CXV setup stiffened the chassis by 10%, plus another 10% when the detachable hardtop was in place, and enabled Morgan to enhance the steering and suspension systems as well. As regards the former, the results included a 13% quicker steering speed backed by improved feedback for the driver. The new suspension, now with standard anti-roll bars and revised geometry, promises "a compliant ride, better body control, and enhanced handling.".

Recent findings suggest that and yes, the Morgan Supersport is available in the U.S. The one major catch, though, is that we only get the four-cylinder model — a 2.0-liter TwinPower turbo-four with 255 horses and 258 pound-feet of torque. It's plenty peppy for a car weighing around 2,500 pounds. But the European Supersport 400 can deliver up to 402 horsepower from its turbocharged 3.0-liter BMW straight-six, taking the Morgan experience to a whole new level.
