Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. New research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

According to recent reports, to investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

Industry observers note that "This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy said. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The fresh analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

Murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

According to recent reports, this effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

In a recent development, "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Sources indicate that researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy remarked.

It has been revealed that but increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

In a recent development, the research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," remarked Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

In a recent development, the growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

According to recent reports, this increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

Sources indicate that "There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's vital that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy said. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study shows that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

According to recent reports, murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

In a recent development, the researchers then initiative to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce vital features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as fresh registry information becomes available each year.

Murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

Industry observers note that current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

According to recent reports, colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

Study Funding and Future Cancer Research.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

According to recent reports, along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

Industry observers note that the University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

#76309. Their HOA Approved Their Backyard Fences. Now They’re Being Told To Tear Them Down.

Their HOA Approved Their Backyard Fences. Now They’re Being Told To Tear Them Down.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that almost six years ago, Laura Burns-Sierra hired Home Depot to install a fence around her property in the Cypress Mill community near Tampa, FL.
  • Now, another organization notes the fence has to come down.
  • It has been revealed that "We couldn't do anything, any construction, any fences, nothing, without HOA approval," Burns-Sierra tells Realtor.com®.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that almost six years ago, Laura Burns-Sierra hired Home Depot to install a fence around her property in the Cypress Mill community near Tampa, FL. She submitted the aims to her homeowners association, received written approval and had the fence professionally installed.

Now, another organization notes the fence has to come down.

It has been revealed that "We couldn't do anything, any construction, any fences, nothing, without HOA approval," Burns-Sierra tells Realtor.com®. "I followed the procedures to the T.".

Sources indicate that burns-Sierra is among a group of homeowners in the Sun City Center neighborhood caught in an unusual dispute between their HOA and the Cypress Mill Community Development District, or CDD. The latter says fences installed within drainage easements are interfering with its ability to maintain the community's stormwater infrastructure and now need to be removed.

The conflict has left residents facing hundreds or even thousands of dollars in unexpected expenses—and raises an important question for homeowners everywhere:.

Is an HOA's written approval enough to protect you when another governing body has authority over your property?

At the center of the dispute is a distinction many homeowners may not realize exists.

In a recent development, an HOA generally oversees community standards, including architectural approvals, landscaping, and fence design. A CDD, meanwhile, is a special-purpose local government that can be responsible for infrastructure such as roads, drainage systems, and stormwater ponds.

In Cypress Mill, those responsibilities overlap on portions of homeowners' properties designated as drainage easements.

Jonathan Ellis, a Florida attorney experienced in HOA law—but is not involved in the dispute directly—tells Realtor.com that HOA approval doesn't necessarily authorize a homeowner to build within an easement.

Sources indicate that "The HOA is telling you we don't have an objection to the fence," Ellis explains. "That doesn't mean now you can build the fence and don't worry about federal law, municipal law, or requirements of the CDD.".

In other words, the HOA may have properly approved the fences under its own rules without resolving whether they complied with the district's separate requirements.

Ellis says the similar names of the HOA and CDD can add to the confusion, particularly for homeowners who aren't familiar with the distinction between the two organizations.

Burns-Sierra indicates the community's drainage ponds had been maintained for years without her fence becoming an concern.

Recent findings suggest that she had her fence installed in May 2021, after receiving written approval from the HOA. About five years later, around Sept. 1, 2026, she and other residents received notice that the structure encroached on a drainage easement and would have to be removed by Sept. 18.

Burns-Sierra says maintenance contractors eventually arrived outside her home prepared to remove her fence and sought $625 for the work.

She refused, saying she wanted time to investigate the district's authority and understand why a fence that had been approved years earlier was suddenly unacceptable.

"I am not going to pay you no money to tear down my fence," she recalls telling the workers.

Neighbor Victor Abreu faced a similar predicament, although his circumstances were different.

Abreu tells Realtor.com that he received written HOA approval to install a gate connecting his home to an existing fence belonging to his neighbor.

When the CDD subsequently demanded that the structures obstructing the drainage easement be removed or relocated, Victor complied.

According to recent reports, on Oct. 19 he paid a contractor $1,000 to install a new section of fencing closer to his house, losing part of a garden he estimates had cost approximately $1,500.

The new arrangement also created a wider opening between neighboring properties, raising concerns about privacy, security, and access to the pond behind their homes.

Victor says he believes communication broke down between the two organizations.

Sources indicate that "I would blame both of them," he states. "I would say 50-50.".

The Cypress Mill CDD maintains that the drainage easements are essential to the neighborhood's stormwater management system.

Recent findings suggest that in a written response to Realtor.com, district counsel Whitney A. Sousa said the ponds and drainage areas are subject to environmental permits and oversight, including requirements administered by the Southwest Florida Water Management District.

The district has a legal responsibility to ensure contractors can inspect, maintain, and repair the system.

Mason Leon, the CDD’s on-site manager, tells Realtor.com that the fencing situation eventually made one pond inaccessible to the district's aquatic maintenance contractor through authorized access routes.

Recent findings suggest that according to Sousa, the issue was brought before the CDD board on Aug. 13, 2026. A subsequent review identified 11 properties with fences or other structures encroaching on drainage easements.

The district determined that the encroachments must be removed to preserve access for maintenance equipment, vehicles, and contractors.

Importantly, Sousa acknowledged that better coordination between the HOA and CDD might have prevented the dispute.

"Ideally, these easements would have been identified during the HOA's review process, and the CDD would have been contacted before the fences were approved or installed," she wrote.

The district plans to work with the HOA to clarify approval requirements going forward.

For homeowners already affected, however, the district expects them to cover the costs of removing or relocating their fences.

According to recent reports, sousa remarked residents requesting additional time have received extensions. The district does not believe those expenses should be spread across the neighborhood through CDD assessments.

Although residents are understandably frustrated, Ellis cautions against assuming the HOA is legally responsible simply because it approved their projects.

"Normally it's the unit owner that's responsible," he indicates, referring to securing all necessary permissions before construction.

Sources indicate that he explains that an HOA's approval generally addresses its own governing documents, including covenants, conditions, and restrictions. It doesn't eliminate the need to comply with separate drainage easements, building regulations, or other legal requirements.

Contractors may also have a role in identifying restrictions before beginning work.

Ellis notes that some communities permit fences within easements on the condition that homeowners remove them when access is needed.

The Cypress Mill CDD, however, has determined that all identified encroachments must be removed.

For homeowners like Burns-Sierra and Abreu, the distinction between an HOA's authority and the district's legal responsibilities has proved expensive.

The dispute offers a cautionary lesson for anyone purchasing a home or planning an outdoor renovation.

Ellis recommends determining which organizations have authority over a property before undertaking improvements.

"Homebuyers want to make sure when they're buying a home that they know of each of the entities that has a say over their property," he notes.

That means checking recorded plats, property surveys, and easement documents before installing fences, patios, pools, or other improvements. Homeowners should also determine whether approvals are required from an HOA, CDD, municipality, county, or utility provider.

And when multiple organizations are involved, written approval from one shouldn't be mistaken for permission from all of them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

Testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

In a recent development, to investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

In a recent development, men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

Sources indicate that A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

Sources indicate that meat protein revealed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

What the Findings Mean for Men's Health.

Despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," states Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

Sources indicate that an important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:29 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

In a recent development, as AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

Industry observers note that “Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”.

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.).

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he stated. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”.

Recent findings suggest that for enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the manufacturer’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that crows can make visual decisions twice as rapidly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • The findings, published in the journal Science, offer fresh insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that crows can make visual decisions twice as rapidly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer fresh insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

Sources indicate that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an notable role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

According to recent reports, the recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

It has been revealed that these signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," indicates Andreas Nieder.

In a recent development, unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#76301. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1584 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an notable difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy.
  • Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.
  • According to recent reports, the findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an notable difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns.

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

It has been revealed that "GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens.".

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies.

It has been revealed that the research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

Recent findings suggest that to make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk.

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, noted the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely crucial findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association.".

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs.

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure key differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

In a recent development, "Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant.".

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish newly introduced clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study.

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

In a recent development, however, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

In a recent development, dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs.".

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance.

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs.".

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an vital risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy.".

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

#76298. Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1411 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread.
  • The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying.
  • It has been revealed that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," mentioned Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises notable questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

It has been revealed that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," mentioned Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals.".

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy.

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish fresh tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal.

In a recent development, the next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

According to recent reports, the study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

Sources indicate that the researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

According to recent reports, this observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

According to recent reports, unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

In a recent development, however, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free.

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

Recent findings suggest that they used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

In a recent development, when fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread.

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments revealed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

It has been revealed that the finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

It has been revealed that cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

Recent findings suggest that "We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," mentioned Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a newly introduced avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

#76296. Breaking: Drought-Stricken Nevada Town Erupts Over Luxury Development’s Plan for ‘Firefighter Pond’

Breaking: Drought-Stricken Nevada Town Erupts Over Luxury Development’s Plan for ‘Firefighter Pond’

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region?
  • That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.
  • Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that should a private developer have the ability to build a human-made pond in the middle of a drought-stricken region? What if that developer indicates that firefighters can access the pond to fight wildfires?

That’s the question at the center of a growing debate in Clark County, NV, where water is scarce and locals are skeptical about a luxury development's plan to create a massive water feature.

Joel Laub and his partner, Randall Jones, began developing the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon in 2022, aiming to create a high-end luxury community amid the Nevada wilderness. The Reserve is being built on 65 acres that were once home to the Bonnie Springs Ranch, a historic, Old West-themed family resort that once featured horseback riding and a small zoo.

According to recent reports, two-acre empty plots in the community start at $7.5 million. But that’s not what has the community up in arms. Instead, it’s what the Reserve is touting on its website: a large human-made pond in the middle of the property.

It has been revealed that to outsiders, it seems like just one feature in a long list of amenities. But for some locals in Clark County, which was declared a natural disaster area due to drought earlier this year, the pond seems like a slap in the face—even as the developers attempt to position it as a fire safety "dip pond.".

“This little dip pond here is really fire safety as an afterthought, and I think that’s pretty obvious in terms of even their planning,” stated Sarah J. McCrea-Dameron, a Blue Diamond, NV, resident and former deputy fire chief from Las Vegas Fire & Rescue, at a zoning commission meeting this past week. “It’s not in an area that’s necessary, and it’s not the best use of that water and that precious resource for our community.“.

It has been revealed that the Reserve at Red Rock Canyon development sits within the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area, an expansive 195,000-acre area within the Mojave Desert. Aztec sandstone foundations dating back to 180 million years can be found in the area, along with sea fossils and hundreds of local bird species. More than 3 million people visit the area each year.

Sources indicate that water for the area is supplied by the Colorado River. In recent years, the river and the several lakes it feeds have been pushed to the limit, as fresh development, coupled with more frequent droughts, have strained resources.

The river doesn’t just supply necessary water to communities across the Southwest: It also produces much-needed hydropower for the region.

Earlier this year, Lake Powell, one of the lakes fed by the Colorado River, dropped to its lowest level in history, threatening to shut down the Glen Canyon Dam, which supplies power to Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Nevada, and Nebraska.

Communities around the Red Rock Canyon Conservation Area take the mantle of water conservation seriously. In fact, in 2020, the nearby community of Blue Diamond issued a temporary moratorium on “the issuance of additional water commitments” that remains in place.

Now, as the developers Laub and Jones offer unbuilt lots in their newly introduced development for $7.5 million, they are pitching the proposed pond as a neighborhood amenity.

“Paths and roads will meander past water features fed by the canyon’s natural springs,” the development’s website states.

Sources indicate that but those types of features are typically prohibited by Clark County’s Title 30, which governs building and development in the area. Title 30 at the moment prohibits the creation of human-made lakes of any size and water features greater than 10 square feet of surface area. So the developers stressed that the human-made pond would be fed via private water rights, and therefore not impede on community resources. Instead of using Colorado River resources, the project would be fed using groundwater.

Bob Gronauer, the developers' lawyer, said the water feature would be a “dip pond”—a water source for use by firefighting helicopters. Wildfires are a frequent problem in the region. In 2025 alone, there were 619 fires in the state, which destroyed more than 368,000 acres.

Industry observers note that in fact, the developers have already signed a use agreement with the Nevada Division of Forestry. The developers claimed the NDF came to them to ask them to create the pond, but the NDF stated the developers approached them about the partnership, the Nevada Independent reported.

"We reached out to the Bureau of Land Management Red Rock management staff at the visitor center, Save Red Rock, Friends of Red Rock, as well as the Nature Conservancy Nevada immediately upon purchasing the property to work with them to make this development compatible with the Red Rock Canyon National Conservation Area," Laub tells Realtor.com. (Laub is the chairman of the Nature Conservancy board.).

Laub states the idea for the dip pond actually came from the BLM.

Recent findings suggest that "They asked if we could work with them on fire management in Red Rock Canyon, and would we consider providing water for firefighting. Of course our answer was yes. We have a 220,000-gallon water tank designed into our water system for supplying water to our fire hydrants, and we agreed to provide a fire hydrant for the BLM water tankers to fill up in the event of a wildfire," Laub continues.

"The ponds are designed to fit into the canyon ecosystem and look natural but also to be compatible with helicopter firefighting.".

Laub tells Realtor.com that they've already been testing the wells in the canyon, and "none of the testing results from these wells has indicated a draw down of significance from our use of the water system.".

He also notes that they purchased the water rights from Bonnie Springs Ranch, which had been in use for more than 60 years.

"The property has had ponds, streams, pools, and springs from the original ranch in 1952," he explains.

To expedite the creation of the dip pools, the developers proposed an amendment to Title 30 that would add language permitting “a body of water, served from standalone private water rights, within 1,000 feet of a National Conservation Area, intended for fire suppression and life safety purposes as agreed upon with a State or Federal Agency.”In October, Clark County Planning Commission's professional staff recommended denying the amendment.

Recent findings suggest that "As proposed, there is no indication of how these water features would be designed, the capacity of these water features, or other potential uses for the stored water. The proliferation of non-essential water features will place an additional burden on the existing water supply," the staff recommendation read. "Furthermore, this request may encourage additional non-essential water features within residential and nonresidential development.".

However, the Planning Commission approved the amendment by a vote of 6-1. It then went to the Clark County Zoning Board for approval. On Wednesday night, during the public comment period of the meeting, around a dozen community members spoke out against the planned feature.

In a recent development, “You can design a decorative water feature and then call it a dip pond. You can offer to let the Forest Service use it knowing that they never will because of the way it’s designed and location, but that doesn’t make that decorative water feature a piece of critical fire infrastructure," remarked former Clark County Fire Capt. Erik Klausen.

“They’re trying to put a plastic fire helmet on this water feature and tell us it’s about public safety,” he continued.

At the end of the public comment period, all seven commissioners voted in favor of the proposed amendment, though, as Commissioner Justin Jones noted, the approval of the amendment does not mean the dip pond project has been approved.

Furthermore, noted Commissioner Marilyn Kirkpatrick, the project needs to be fit for purpose.

Industry observers note that "If it's a fire-suppression pond, then it has to be a fire-suppression pond in my mind," remarked Kirkpatrick. "It should stay as a fire-supression pond, not as a recreational venue, not as irrigation, because that water is supposed to be there for a reason.".

Realtor.com has reached out to developer Jones and lawyer Gronauer for comment.

#76295. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2934 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia Corp.
  • Revenue more than doubled year-over-year.
  • This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:32 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the organization’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly stated he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”.

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

It has been revealed that the fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress stated the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

In a recent development, she explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

Industry observers note that I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The manufacturer’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Industry observers note that earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Industry observers note that employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the manufacturer held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

Industry observers note that for information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

According to recent reports, one of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he mentioned the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our latest CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”.

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the organization “still has some time to study.”.

It has been revealed that huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

According to recent reports, for IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The newly introduced Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

It has been revealed that with demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress remarked. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”.

Recent findings suggest that those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress noted the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so swiftly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Sources indicate that over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain key, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She remarked Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”.

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

It has been revealed that “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”.

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

In a recent development, the flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

It has been revealed that my advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

Recent findings suggest that the demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

In a recent development, the CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive fresh spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress noted, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom reveals how promptly the workload is changing.

In a recent development, nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress noted co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, blueprint CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

Recent findings suggest that the question of who the latest CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the organization.

Recent findings suggest that most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:.

It has been revealed that matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

In a recent development, jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves rapidly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management tech giant. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the organization can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an key hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

In a recent development, this call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Industry observers note that kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.
